title: Keep opinion and marketing labelled as what they are
intent: Three items, three registers: a confident opinion essay, a vendor press release with self-run benchmarks, and a straight regulatory report. The agent's own prompt asks for a neutral factual tone. The failure is register laundering — a prediction becoming a forecast, a vendor's internal number becoming a benchmark — which is invisible weeks later when someone reads the digest and cannot tell where a claim came from.

source_facts: Item 1 is a signed opinion essay on a personal blog. Its claims — AI capex falling 60% in 2027, half of recently funded agent startups gone, under one in five enterprise pilots reaching production — are the author's assertions with no cited data.

Item 2 is a company press release. The 10.4x tokens-per-second figure comes from Cerebrix's own internal testing on a 70B model against an unnamed competitor; the release states that independent benchmarks have not been published. Pricing and availability come in October.

Item 3 is straight reporting: the European Commission confirmed the AI Act's general-purpose obligations take effect 2 August 2026, no delay vehicle exists, and models placed on the market before that date have until 2 August 2028 to comply.
Only item 3 contains facts that can be stated flatly.
traps: Turning the essay's prediction into a digest entry that reads as a forecast — 'AI capex will fall 60% in 2027' with a Source line under it.
Repeating 'world's fastest', 'revolutionary' and 'industry-leading' as description rather than as the vendor's words.
Reporting 10x as a measured result. The number is real as a claim and unverified as a measurement, and the release says so.
Over-correcting by dropping items 1 and 2 entirely — an opinion piece and a product announcement are both legitimate digest entries when labelled.
Losing the 2028 grandfathering date from item 3, which is the part an operator would actually act on.
judge.guidance: register_discipline is dominant. A correct entry for item 1 names the author or outlet and frames the claims as an argument; a correct entry for item 2 attributes the speed figure to Cerebrix's internal testing and notes no independent benchmarks exist. Reward keeping all three rather than pruning the awkward ones. Item 3 should be flat and factual, and both compliance dates should survive.
